Overview

SentinelLABS and Censys measured how many Ollama servers, which bind to localhost by default but are one setting away from the open internet, are publicly reachable. Over 293 days they recorded 7.23 million observations of 175,108 unique hosts in 130 countries and 4,032 autonomous systems. The population is bimodal: hosts seen more than 100 times are 13% of hosts but 76% of observations, around a persistent core the summary puts at 23,000. By network tier, hyperscalers and telecom or residential networks each hold 32% of hosts, and about a fifth cannot be attributed at all. Model choice is concentrated: Llama, Qwen2 and Gemma2 rank first to third under every weighting, the Q4_K_M quantization runs on 48% of hosts, and 4-bit formats make up 72% of quantizations. Capabilities matter more than counts: 48% of hosts advertise tool calling, 22% vision and 26% reasoning models, at least 201 run standard "uncensored" system prompts, and about 5,000 combine high capability with 87% average uptime. The security section names five risks: free compute for spam, phishing or disinformation; tool-enabled and retrieval-backed hosts that answer anyone's prompts; residential addresses that launder malicious traffic; a monoculture that one flaw could hit at once; and owners who cannot be identified or reached. The authors call the result a governance inversion, with deployment scattered across home networks while dependency concentrates on a few labs' models, and they conclude that exposed LLM endpoints need the same authentication, monitoring and network controls as any other internet-facing service.

Limits

  • Exposure, not exploitation. It counts reachable hosts and their advertised capabilities; it reports no observed abuse of them, and its threat vectors are argued.
  • Method in outline only. Scan cadence, how a host was identified as Ollama, and how capabilities and system prompts were queried are not described in detail, and the "uncensored" count is a stated lower bound.
  • A joint study with the scan provider. One author is from Censys, whose data it uses.
  • Read from an archive. sentinelone.com answered scripted requests with HTTP 429 on 2026-11-02; the digest is of the Internet Archive's copy of 2026-03-02, and the live page may have changed since.

Published attacksadjacentAIT-040, AIT-113, AIT-051, AIT-064AIT-040 and AIT-113 cite it. It measures the reachable surface AIT-040 attacks, but demonstrates and reports no exploitation. Its compute-abuse scenario needs no credentials, since the hosts are unauthenticated, so it fits AIT-113 (stolen keys and credentials) only loosely. Links that are ours: prompting a reachable retrieval deployment for data such as API keys (AIT-051) and indirect prompt injection through images on vision-capable hosts (AIT-064), both argued, not shown
